source.text: הַדָּבָ֞ר אֲשֶׁר־הָיָ֤ה עַֽל־יִרְמְיָ֨הוּ֙ עַל־כָּל־עַ֣ם יְהוּדָ֔ה בַּשָּׁנָה֙ הָֽרְבִעִ֔ית לִיהוֹיָקִ֥ים בֶּן־יֹאשִׁיָּ֖הוּ מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֑ה הִ֗יא הַשָּׁנָה֙ הָרִ֣אשֹׁנִ֔ית לִנְבֽוּכַדְרֶאצַּ֖ר מֶ֥לֶךְ בָּבֶֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all [the] people of Judah in the year the fourth of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, it [was] the year the first of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon,

en.L: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah (that [was] the first year of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon),
en.B: This message came to Jeremiah about all the people of Judah in the fourth year of the reign of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, in what was also the first year of the reign of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon.
en.R: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} gave Jeremiah a message about all the people of Judah. It came in the fourth year that Jehoiakim son of Josiah was king of Judah. That was the first year that Nebuchadrezzar was king of Babylon.

decisions.choice: the fourth year of Jehoiakim, the first year of Nebuchadrezzar: 605 BC
decisions.reason: Jehoiakim became king in 609 BC, so his fourth year was 605 BC. That was the year Nebuchadrezzar defeated Egypt at Carchemish (46:2, dated to the same year) and succeeded his father as king of Babylon. This is the first time Jeremiah dates a message by a foreign king's reign: from now on Babylon sets the calendar for Judah. The same year is the setting of chapter 36 (36:1) and of chapter 45. Daniel 1:1 speaks of the third year of Jehoiakim for Nebuchadnezzar's first move against Jerusalem; that probably counts Jehoiakim's years from his first full year rather than from his accession. The Greek translation lacks the words "that was the first year of Nebuchadrezzar" (see the note at 1:1; this is from general knowledge).

decisions.choice: the word ... concerning all the people of Judah: a message about them and addressed to them
decisions.reason: The phrase introduces a message about the whole people; verse 2 adds that Jeremiah spoke it to them. It is the summing up of his preaching up to this point (verse 3).

decisions.choice: Nebuchadrezzar: the form of the name with r, kept as the Hebrew has it here
decisions.reason: Jeremiah and Ezekiel mostly spell the king's name Nebuchadrezzar, close to the Babylonian Nabu-kudurri-usur ("Nabu, protect my heir"). Kings, Chronicles, Daniel and a few places in Jeremiah (27-29) spell it Nebuchadnezzar. Both name the same king, who reigned 605-562 BC.

decisions.choice: Nebuchadrezzar
decisions.reason: Each verse keeps the form of the name its Hebrew uses, so readers can see the two spellings; m3 explains that they are one man.

decisions.choice: a parenthesis (Literal); a relative clause (Balanced); a separate sentence (Readable); a comma at the end of the verse (Literal)
decisions.reason: The second date explains the first. The sentence runs on into verse 2, so Literal ends with a comma; Balanced and Readable finish the date here and let verse 2 begin a new sentence. Balanced uses the book's heading wording ("This message came to Jeremiah") and the dating formula "in the fourth year of the reign of", and Readable says plainly that the LORD gave the message.

source.text: אֲשֶׁ֨ר דִּבֶּ֜ר יִרְמְיָ֤הוּ הַנָּבִיא֙ עַל־כָּל־עַ֣ם יְהוּדָ֔ה וְאֶ֛ל כָּל־יֹשְׁבֵ֥י יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם לֵאמֹֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: which spoke Jeremiah the prophet to all [the] people of Judah and to all [the] inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying:

en.L: which Jeremiah the prophet spoke to all the people of Judah and to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying:
en.B: Jeremiah the prophet spoke it to all the people of Judah and to everyone living in Jerusalem. He said:
en.R: Jeremiah the prophet told it to all the people of Judah and to everyone who lived in Jerusalem. He said:

decisions.choice: which Jeremiah spoke: the message of verse 1, now delivered by the prophet to the people
decisions.reason: The relative word picks up "the word" of verse 1. Verses 3-14 are Jeremiah's own speech, in which he reports what the LORD has said.

decisions.choice: saying: (Literal); He said: (Balanced, Readable), with Jeremiah's speech opening in verse 3
decisions.reason: Jeremiah's speech runs from verse 3 to verse 14, so its quotation marks open at verse 3 and close at verse 14.

source.text: מִן־שְׁלֹ֣שׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֣ה שָׁנָ֡ה לְיֹאשִׁיָּ֣הוּ בֶן־אָמוֹן֩ מֶ֨לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֜ה וְעַ֣ד׀הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֗ה זֶ֚ה שָׁלֹ֤שׁ וְעֶשְׂרִים֙ שָׁנָ֔ה הָיָ֥ה דְבַר־יְהוָ֖ה אֵלָ֑י וָאֲדַבֵּ֧ר אֲלֵיכֶ֛ם אַשְׁכֵּ֥ים וְדַבֵּ֖ר וְלֹ֥א שְׁמַעְתֶּֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: From thirteen year of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah, and until the day this, this three and twenty year[s] has come [the] word of Yahweh to me, and I have spoken to you, rising early and speaking, and not you have listened.

en.L: "From the thirteenth year of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah, until this day, these twenty-three years, the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has come to me, and I have spoken to you, rising early and speaking, and you have not listened.
en.B: "For twenty-three years, from the thirteenth year of the reign of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah, up to this very day, the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has come to me. Again and again I have spoken to you, but you have not listened.
en.R: "For twenty-three years {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has been giving me {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} messages. It began in the thirteenth year that Josiah son of Amon was king of Judah, and it has gone on until today. I have told you {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} messages over and over, but you have not listened.

decisions.choice: twenty-three years: from 627 BC to 605 BC, counting both the first and the last year
decisions.reason: Jeremiah's call came in Josiah's thirteenth year (1:2). Josiah reigned thirty-one years (2 Kings 22:1), which leaves nineteen years of his reign; Jehoahaz reigned three months, and this is Jehoiakim's fourth year (verse 1). Counted the ancient way, with the first and last years both included, that gives twenty-three years.

decisions.choice: rising early and speaking: speaking again and again, without giving up
decisions.reason: As in 7:13. The form of the first verb here is unusual (it looks like an Aramaic spelling), but the phrase is the one Jeremiah uses throughout for God's untiring warnings.

decisions.choice: I have spoken ... you have not listened: the prophet's whole ministry summed up as one long appeal refused
decisions.reason: The perfect verbs look back over the whole twenty-three years. Verse 4 sets the LORD's sending of all his prophets beside Jeremiah's own preaching.

decisions.choice: rising early and speaking (L); again and again (B); over and over (R)
decisions.reason: The wording set for this phrase throughout Jeremiah.

decisions.choice: giving me his messages ... told you his messages
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "the word of the LORD came to me" means (as at 1:2), and that what Jeremiah spoke was that message.

source.text: וְשָׁלַח֩ יְהוָ֨ה אֲלֵיכֶ֜ם אֶֽת־כָּל־עֲבָדָ֧יו הַנְּבִאִ֛ים הַשְׁכֵּ֥ם וְשָׁלֹ֖חַ וְלֹ֣א שְׁמַעְתֶּ֑ם וְלֹֽא־הִטִּיתֶ֥ם אֶֽת־אָזְנְכֶ֖ם לִשְׁמֹֽעַ׃

records.literal_gloss: And sent Yahweh to you all his servants the prophets, rising early and sending, and not you listened, and not you inclined your ear to hear,

en.L: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has sent to you all {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} servants the prophets, rising early and sending [them], but you have not listened, nor have you inclined your ear to hear,
en.B: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has sent you all {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} servants the prophets again and again, but you have not listened or even paid attention.
en.R: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has also sent you all {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} servants the prophets, over and over. But you would not listen. You would not even pay attention.

decisions.choice: his servants the prophets: those who served God by bringing his word
decisions.reason: As in 7:25. Jeremiah was not alone: the LORD had sent prophet after prophet with the same call (2 Kings 17:13).

decisions.choice: rising early and sending: sending them constantly
decisions.reason: As in 7:25.

decisions.choice: you did not incline your ear: you did not even turn to listen
decisions.reason: To bend the ear toward someone is to give attention. The people refused even the first step of hearing (7:24, 26; 11:8).

decisions.choice: servants
decisions.reason: As in 7:25, "servant" is kept at every level when the word names those who serve God.

decisions.choice: rising early and sending (L); again and again (B); over and over (R); inclined your ear (L); paid attention (B, R)
decisions.reason: The set wording for the first phrase; Balanced and Readable give the sense of the ear idiom. The Literal sentence runs on into verse 5 and ends with a comma.

source.text: לֵאמֹ֗ר שֽׁוּבוּ־נָ֞א אִ֣ישׁ מִדַּרְכּ֤וֹ הָֽרָעָה֙ וּמֵרֹ֣עַ מַעַלְלֵיכֶ֔ם וּשְׁבוּ֙ עַל־הָ֣אֲדָמָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֨ר נָתַ֧ן יְהוָ֛ה לָכֶ֖ם וְלַאֲבֽוֹתֵיכֶ֑ם לְמִן־עוֹלָ֖ם וְעַד־עוֹלָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: saying: Turn please each from his way the evil and from [the] evil of your deeds, and dwell on the land which gave Yahweh to you and to your fathers from of old and until forever.

en.L: saying, 'Turn now, each one from {{gender:their|his}} evil way and from the evil of your deeds, and dwell in the land that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave to you and to your fathers from of old and forever.
en.B: They said, 'Turn back, every one of you, from your evil ways and your evil deeds, and you will live in the land that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave to you and your ancestors to keep for all time.
en.R: The prophets told you, 'Each of you must stop living in your evil ways and doing evil things. Then you can live in the land that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave to you and to your ancestors, to be yours forever.

decisions.choice: turn: repent, come back from evil to the LORD
decisions.reason: The verb is Jeremiah's key word for repentance (3:12, 14, 22; 18:11). It means a turning of the whole life, here from evil ways and deeds.

decisions.choice: and dwell: the result promised to those who turn
decisions.reason: The second command follows the first as its outcome: turn, and you will live in the land. The same promise stands in the temple sermon (7:3, 7).

decisions.choice: from of old and forever: the land given for all time
decisions.reason: The double phrase covers the whole span from the gift to the ancestors on into the future, as in 7:7. The gift was lasting, but living in it depended on faithfulness.

decisions.choice: single quotation marks for the prophets' words, inside Jeremiah's speech
decisions.reason: Jeremiah quotes what the prophets said, so their words take single quotation marks. Balanced and Readable begin a new sentence and supply "They said" or "The prophets told you"; Readable also supplies "must" and "Then" to show that living in the land depended on turning. Literal follows 18:11 for "each one from their evil way", with the gender setting, since the call is to men and women alike.

source.text: וְאַל־תֵּלְכ֗וּ אַֽחֲרֵי֙ אֱלֹהִ֣ים אֲחֵרִ֔ים לְעָבְדָ֖ם וּלְהִשְׁתַּחֲוֺ֣ת לָהֶ֑ם וְלֹֽא־תַכְעִ֤יסוּ אוֹתִי֙ בְּמַעֲשֵׂ֣ה יְדֵיכֶ֔ם וְלֹ֥א אָרַ֖ע לָכֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And not go after gods other to serve them and to bow down to them, and not provoke me with [the] work of your hands, and not I will do harm to you.

en.L: And do not go after other gods to serve them and to bow down to them, and do not provoke {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} to anger with the work of your hands; then I will do you no harm.'
en.B: Do not follow other gods to serve and worship them. Do not make {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} angry with the idols your hands have made, and I will not harm you.'
en.R: Do not follow other gods. Do not serve them or bow down to worship them. Do not make {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} angry by worshiping idols you have made with your own hands. If you obey, I will not punish you.'

decisions.choice: go after other gods: give loyalty to other gods
decisions.reason: To go after someone is to follow them as one's master. The phrase comes from the covenant warnings (Deuteronomy 6:14; 8:19) and runs through Jeremiah (7:6, 9; 11:10).

decisions.choice: the work of your hands: idols made by human hands
decisions.reason: The phrase means the idols, things people make and then worship (1:16; Deuteronomy 4:28). It could also mean their deeds in general, but beside "other gods" the idols are meant.

decisions.choice: provoke me ... I will do you no harm: God speaks in his own voice inside the prophets' message
decisions.reason: The prophets spoke God's words in his name, so the message they gave says "me" and "I" of God.

decisions.choice: If you obey, I will not punish you
decisions.reason: Readable supplies "If you obey" to show the condition, and says "punish" for the harm God would bring as judgment.

source.text: וְלֹֽא־שְׁמַעְתֶּ֥ם אֵלַ֖י נְאֻם־יְהוָ֑ה לְמַ֧עַן הַכְעִיסֵ֛נִי בְּמַעֲשֵׂ֥ה יְדֵיכֶ֖ם לְרַ֥ע לָכֶֽם׃ס

records.literal_gloss: But not you have listened to me, declaration of Yahweh, so as to provoke me with [the] work of your hands to harm to you.

en.L: But you have not listened to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, so that you have provoked {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} to anger with the work of your hands, to your own harm.
en.B: But you have not listened to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. You have made {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} angry with the idols your hands have made, and brought harm on yourselves.
en.R: But you would not listen to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. You made {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} angry with the idols you made, and so you have brought trouble on yourselves.

decisions.choice: you have not listened to me, declares the LORD: Jeremiah speaks God's words in God's own voice
decisions.reason: Jeremiah's report of his preaching turns into the LORD's own words, marked by "declares the LORD". There is no new quotation in the Hebrew; the prophet speaks for God.

decisions.choice: so that you provoked me ... to your harm: the result of their refusal, which turns back on themselves
decisions.reason: The word "so that" here marks what came of their actions, not their purpose. They angered God, and the harm fell on them. The Hebrew has a written form "so as to provoke me" with a marginal reading "they provoked me"; the sense is the same either way.

decisions.choice: declares (L, B); says (R)
decisions.reason: The set wording for this formula, as in Isaiah. Balanced and Readable break the verse into shorter sentences.

source.text: לָכֵ֕ן כֹּ֥ה אָמַ֖ר יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֑וֹת יַ֕עַן אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹֽא־שְׁמַעְתֶּ֖ם אֶת־דְּבָרָֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: Therefore thus says Yahweh of hosts: Because that not you have listened to my words,

en.L: Therefore thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts: Because you have not listened to {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} words,
en.B: So {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies says this: Because you have not listened to {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} words,
en.R: So this is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies says: You have not listened to what I said.

decisions.choice: therefore: the judgment that follows from twenty-three years of refusal
decisions.reason: The word links the sentence of judgment (verses 8-11) to the refusal described in verses 3-7. Inside Jeremiah's speech the LORD's words now follow directly.

decisions.choice: listened to: obeyed
decisions.reason: To listen to someone's words is to do what they say. The same verb runs through verses 3, 4 and 7.

decisions.choice: the LORD of Armies
decisions.reason: As in Isaiah, Balanced and Readable say "Armies" for "hosts" (see Isaiah 1:9).

decisions.choice: a separate sentence
decisions.reason: Readable makes the reason its own sentence; verse 9 then states what God will do. Literal and Balanced keep the Hebrew sentence running into verse 9.

source.text: הִנְנִ֣י שֹׁלֵ֡חַ וְלָקַחְתִּי֩ אֶת־כָּל־מִשְׁפְּח֨וֹת צָפ֜וֹן נְאֻם־יְהוָ֗ה וְאֶל־נְבֽוּכַדְרֶאצַּ֣ר מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶל֮ עַבְדִּי֒ וַהֲבִ֨אֹתִ֜ים עַל־הָאָ֤רֶץ הַזֹּאת֙ וְעַל־יֹ֣שְׁבֶ֔יהָ וְעַ֛ל כָּל־הַגּוֹיִ֥ם הָאֵ֖לֶּה סָבִ֑יב וְהַ֣חֲרַמְתִּ֔ים וְשַׂמְתִּים֙ לְשַׁמָּ֣ה וְלִשְׁרֵקָ֔ה וּלְחָרְב֖וֹת עוֹלָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: here I [am] sending and I will take all [the] clans of [the] north, declaration of Yahweh, and to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon my servant, and I will bring them on the land this and on its inhabitants and on all the nations these around, and I will devote them to destruction and I will make them into a horror and into a hissing and into ruins of forever.

en.L: look, I am sending and I will take all the clans of the north, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and [I am sending] to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} servant, and I will bring them against this land and against its inhabitants and against all these nations around [it]; and I will devote them to destruction, and I will make them a horror and a hissing and everlasting ruins.
en.B: I am going to send for all the peoples of the north, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and for Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} servant. I will bring them against this land and its people and against all the nations around it. I will devote them to destruction and make them a horror, an object of scorn, and ruins forever.
en.R: I am going to send for all the peoples from the north, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. I will send for {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} servant Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon. I will bring them to attack this land and the people who live here, and all the nations around you. I will destroy them all completely. People will be horrified at them and mock them. Those places will lie in ruins forever.

decisions.choice: Nebuchadrezzar ... my servant: the foreign king is God's instrument, carrying out God's purpose
alternatives: my servant meaning a worshiper of God
decisions.reason: God calls the king of Babylon "my servant" here and in 27:6 and 43:10. The title does not mean that Nebuchadrezzar worshiped Israel's God or was good. It means that he did God's work, the way a servant carries out his master's orders: he would bring the judgment God had decreed. Isaiah says something similar of Assyria as the rod of God's anger (Isaiah 10:5-7) and of Cyrus as God's anointed (Isaiah 45:1). The title also tells Judah that resisting Babylon is resisting God (27:6-8). The Greek translation lacks "Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon my servant" here (see the note at 1:1; this is from general knowledge).

decisions.choice: all the clans of the north: the peoples who make up the army from the north
decisions.reason: The enemy from the north was announced in Jeremiah's call (1:14-15, where the same clans are named) and in the poems of chapters 4-6 (4:6; 6:22). Here, for the first time, that enemy is named: Babylon and its allies.

decisions.choice: devote them to destruction: give them over wholly to destruction as under God's ban
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used for the ban, the total destruction of what is given over to God (Deuteronomy 7:2; Joshua 6:21). What Israel once did to the nations of Canaan God now does to Judah and its neighbors.

decisions.choice: a horror and a hissing: a sight that appalls, at which people whistle in shock and scorn
decisions.reason: As in 19:8. Hissing or whistling at a ruin showed shock and contempt (18:16; 1 Kings 9:8). "Everlasting ruins" means ruins that will stand for a very long time.

decisions.choice: servant (every level)
decisions.reason: The style guide gives "slave" at Literal for this word. Here, as in Isaiah, the word names one who carries out God's purpose (see m1), and Jeremiah uses the same title for God's prophets (verse 4), so "servant" is kept at every level. "Slave" would suggest that the point is the king's lowly status, when the point is the task God has given him.

decisions.choice: devote to destruction (L, B), destroy completely (R); a horror and a hissing (L), a horror, an object of scorn (B), horrified ... mock (R)
decisions.reason: The set wording for the ban and for this list. Readable spells the list out in short sentences. Literal supplies "[I am sending]" and "[it]", which the Hebrew leaves understood.

source.text: וְהַאֲבַדְתִּ֣י מֵהֶ֗ם ק֤וֹל שָׂשׂוֹן֙ וְק֣וֹל שִׂמְחָ֔ה ק֥וֹל חָתָ֖ן וְק֣וֹל כַּלָּ֑ה ק֥וֹל רֵחַ֖יִם וְא֥וֹר נֵֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And I will make perish from them [the] sound of joy and [the] sound of gladness, [the] voice of bridegroom and [the] voice of bride, [the] sound of millstones and [the] light of lamp.

en.L: And I will banish from them the sound of joy and the sound of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the sound of the millstones and the light of the lamp.
en.B: I will take away from them the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of bridegroom and bride, the grinding of the millstones and the light of the lamp.
en.R: I will end the sounds of joy and happiness among them. No one will hear the happy voices of a bride and groom at their wedding. No one will hear the sound of grain being ground at the mill. No one will see the light of a lamp in their homes.

decisions.choice: the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride: the joy of weddings, the sound of ordinary happy life
decisions.reason: As in 7:34 and 16:9. This verse adds two more signs of daily life to the list.

decisions.choice: the sound of the millstones and the light of the lamp: daily bread and a lived-in home
decisions.reason: Every household ground its grain each morning with a pair of hand millstones, and a small oil lamp burned in the house at night. When both stop, no one is left to bake bread or keep a home. Revelation 18:22-23 takes up the same pictures for the fall of Babylon.

decisions.choice: I will make perish: I will put an end to these sounds completely
decisions.reason: The verb means to destroy or make vanish. 7:34 says "I will make cease" with another verb; the sense is the same.

decisions.choice: the wording of 7:34 for joy, gladness, bridegroom and bride
decisions.reason: The same list keeps the same words at each level as in 7:34. Readable explains the millstones (grain being ground) and says that the lamps are in their homes.

source.text: וְהָֽיְתָה֙ כָּל־הָאָ֣רֶץ הַזֹּ֔את לְחָרְבָּ֖ה לְשַׁמָּ֑ה וְעָ֨בְד֜וּ הַגּוֹיִ֥ם הָאֵ֛לֶּה אֶת־מֶ֥לֶךְ בָּבֶ֖ל שִׁבְעִ֥ים שָׁנָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And will become all the land this a ruin, a horror, and will serve the nations these [the] king of Babylon seventy year[s].

en.L: And this whole land will become a ruin [and] a horror, and these nations will serve the king of Babylon seventy years.
en.B: This whole land will become a desolate ruin, and for seventy years these nations will serve the king of Babylon.
en.R: This whole land will become an empty ruin, a terrible sight. These nations will serve the king of Babylon for seventy years.

decisions.choice: seventy years: the full span set for Babylon's rule, after which God will act
alternatives: an exact count of seventy years
a round number for a lifetime
decisions.reason: Seventy years is a full lifetime (Psalm 90:10) and a round number for a complete period (Isaiah 23:15 says the same of Tyre). Babylon's rule over the region lasted from about 605 BC, the year of this message, until Babylon fell to Cyrus in 539 BC, close to seventy years. Others count from the temple's destruction in 586 BC to its rebuilding in 516 BC, exactly seventy. The number returns in 29:10, where it marks the time before the exiles return. 2 Chronicles 36:21 reads it as the land keeping its missed sabbaths (Leviticus 26:34-35), Zechariah 1:12 and 7:5 count it in their own day, and Daniel 9:2 tells of Daniel reading this prophecy and praying, with an answer that speaks of seventy weeks (Daniel 9:24). The text gives a set time; how its years were counted is not stated.

decisions.choice: a ruin, a horror: a desolate land that appalls those who see it
decisions.reason: The second word is the one translated "horror" in verse 9. Of a land it describes both the desolation and the shock of those who see it.

decisions.choice: these nations: Judah and the neighboring nations named in verse 9
decisions.reason: "These nations" points back to the nations around Judah in verse 9; Judah is included with them under Babylon.

decisions.choice: a desolate ruin (B); an empty ruin, a terrible sight (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced joins the two nouns into one phrase; Readable keeps both ideas, the emptiness and the shock.

source.text: וְהָיָ֣ה כִמְלֹ֣אות שִׁבְעִ֣ים שָׁנָ֡ה אֶפְקֹ֣ד עַל־מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶל֩ וְעַל־הַגּ֨וֹי הַה֧וּא נְאֻם־יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־עֲוֺנָ֖ם וְעַל־אֶ֣רֶץ כַּשְׂדִּ֑ים וְשַׂמְתִּ֥י אֹת֖וֹ לְשִֽׁמְמ֥וֹת עוֹלָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And it will be, when are completed seventy year[s], I will visit on [the] king of Babylon and on the nation that, declaration of Yahweh, their iniquity, and on [the] land of [the] Chaldeans, and I will make it desolations of forever.

en.L: And it will be, when seventy years are completed, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, for their iniquity, and the land of the Chaldeans, and I will make it an everlasting desolation.
en.B: But when the seventy years are over, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation for their guilt, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. I will punish the land of the Chaldeans and make it a desolation forever.
en.R: But when the seventy years are over, I will punish the king of Babylon and his nation for their sins, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. I will punish the land of the Babylonians and make it an empty waste forever.

decisions.choice: I will visit on ... their iniquity: I will punish them for their guilt
decisions.reason: To "visit" a sin on someone is to bring its punishment on them (5:9; Exodus 20:5). Babylon was God's instrument, but it would answer for its own cruelty and pride (50:29-32; 51:24).

decisions.choice: when seventy years are completed: the limit God has set to Babylon's rule
decisions.reason: See verse 11. The judgment on Judah has an end, and the nation that brought it will be judged in turn; chapters 50-51 spell this out.

decisions.choice: the land of the Chaldeans: Babylonia
decisions.reason: The Chaldeans were the people of southern Mesopotamia whose kings ruled Babylon in Jeremiah's time, so the name stands for the Babylonians.

decisions.choice: iniquity (L), guilt (B), sins (R); Chaldeans (L, B), Babylonians (R)
decisions.reason: The set wording for these terms, as in Isaiah. Balanced and Readable repeat "I will punish" before the land to make the sentence clear.

source.text: וְהֵֽבֵאתִי֙ עַל־הָאָ֣רֶץ הַהִ֔יא אֶת־כָּל־דְּבָרַ֖י אֲשֶׁר־דִּבַּ֣רְתִּי עָלֶ֑יהָ אֵ֤ת כָּל־הַכָּתוּב֙ בַּסֵּ֣פֶר הַזֶּ֔ה אֲשֶׁר־נִבָּ֥א יִרְמְיָ֖הוּ עַל־כָּל־הַגּוֹיִֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And I will bring on the land that all my words which I have spoken against it, all the [thing] written in the book this, which prophesied Jeremiah against all the nations.

en.L: And I will bring on that land all {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} words that I have spoken against it, all that is written in this book, which Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations.
en.B: I will bring on that land everything I have said against it, all that is written in this book, which Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations.
en.R: I will make everything I have said against Babylon come true. All of it is written in this book. It is what Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations.

decisions.choice: the Hebrew order, in which the oracles against the nations come later in the book (chapters 46-51)
alternatives: the Greek order, with the oracles against the nations following here
decisions.reason: This is the point at which the Greek translation of Jeremiah places its oracles against the nations, which the Hebrew gives as chapters 46-51. In the Greek, the words "which Jeremiah prophesied against the nations" serve as the heading of those oracles, and the Greek lacks verse 14. See the note at 1:1. This translation follows the Hebrew order. These statements come from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: which Jeremiah prophesied: words that speak of Jeremiah in the third person, inside God's speech
decisions.reason: God has been speaking in the first person ("my words"), and here Jeremiah is named as the one who prophesied. The clause reads like a note that describes the book, joined to God's words; it shows that the prophet's messages were already being gathered in writing (compare 36:2, 32, dated to the same year).

decisions.choice: that land: Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans in verse 12
decisions.reason: "That land" and "against it" refer to the land of the Chaldeans just named.

decisions.choice: Babylon
decisions.reason: Readable names the land so that no reader takes "that land" to be Judah.

source.text: כִּ֣י עָֽבְדוּ־בָ֤ם גַּם־הֵ֨מָּה֙ גּוֹיִ֣ם רַבִּ֔ים וּמְלָכִ֖ים גְּדוֹלִ֑ים וְשִׁלַּמְתִּ֥י לָהֶ֛ם כְּפָעֳלָ֖ם וּכְמַעֲשֵׂ֥ה יְדֵיהֶֽם׃ס

records.literal_gloss: For will make serve them also they nations many and kings great, and I will repay them according to their deed[s] and according to [the] work of their hands.

en.L: For many nations and great kings will make slaves of them also, and I will repay them according to their deeds and according to the work of their hands."
en.B: For many nations and great kings will make them serve in their turn, and I will repay them for what they have done, for the work of their hands."
en.R: Many nations and great kings will force the Babylonians to serve them, as they forced others to serve. I will pay them back for all the evil things they have done."

decisions.choice: will make slaves of them also: those who subjected the nations will in turn be subjected
decisions.reason: The same verb "serve" used in verse 11 of the nations serving Babylon now turns on Babylon itself. "Also they" stresses the reversal (27:7; 50:9; 51:27-28).

decisions.choice: according to their deeds and the work of their hands: in full measure for what they did
decisions.reason: The pair of phrases means all their conduct. "The work of their hands" here means their deeds, not idols as in verses 6-7 (50:29).

decisions.choice: make slaves of (L); make ... serve (B, R)
decisions.reason: The style guide gives "slave" at Literal and "make ... serve" at Balanced and Readable for the verb of enslaving. Readable names the Babylonians and supplies "as they forced others to serve" to show the reversal.

decisions.choice: Jeremiah's speech closes here
decisions.reason: The quotation that opened at verse 3 ends with this verse. Verse 15 begins a new account.

source.text: כִּ֣י כֹה֩ אָמַ֨ר יְהוָ֜ה אֱלֹהֵ֤י יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ אֵלַ֔י קַ֠ח אֶת־כּ֨וֹס הַיַּ֧יִן הַחֵמָ֛ה הַזֹּ֖את מִיָּדִ֑י וְהִשְׁקִיתָ֤ה אֹתוֹ֙ אֶת־כָּל־הַגּוֹיִ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֧ר אָנֹכִ֛י שֹׁלֵ֥חַ אוֹתְךָ֖ אֲלֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: For thus said Yahweh [the] God of Israel to me: Take the cup of the wine, the wrath, this from my hand, and make drink it all the nations that I [am] sending you to them.

en.L: For thus {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, said to me: "Take this cup of the wine of wrath from {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} hand, and make all the nations to whom I am sending you drink it.
en.B: For {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, said this to me: "Take this cup filled with the wine of {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} wrath from {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} hand, and make all the nations I am sending you to drink it.
en.R: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, said to me, "Here is a cup in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} hand. It is filled with wine, and the wine is {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} anger. Take it. Then go to all the nations I am sending you to, and make them drink it.

decisions.choice: the cup of the wine of wrath: God's judgment pictured as a cup the nations must drink
decisions.reason: The cup that makes those who drink it reel is a common picture of God's judgment: Psalm 75:9; Isaiah 51:17, 22; Habakkuk 2:16; Lamentations 4:21; Ezekiel 23:31-33. Jeremiah returns to it in 49:12 and 51:7, where Babylon itself is the cup in God's hand. Revelation takes it up in the "wine of God's wrath" (Revelation 14:10; 16:19).

decisions.choice: the wine, the wrath: wine that is God's wrath
decisions.reason: The two nouns stand side by side, "the wine, the wrath". The second explains the first: the wine is God's anger. It is not wine poured out because of wrath, but wrath itself given as drink.

decisions.choice: take ... and make them drink: a prophetic sign, whose manner is not described
decisions.reason: The text does not say whether Jeremiah carried a cup to the kings of all these nations, saw it in a vision, or acted it out in Jerusalem before their envoys (compare 27:2-3). What matters is that his word carries God's judgment to the nations, as his call said (1:10).

decisions.choice: filled with the wine of my wrath (B); the wine is my anger (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "my" because the cup is from God's hand and the wrath is his. Readable unfolds the picture in short sentences. The LORD's words to Jeremiah open a quotation that closes at the end of verse 16.

source.text: וְשָׁת֕וּ וְהִֽתְגֹּֽעֲשׁ֖וּ וְהִתְהֹלָ֑לוּ מִפְּנֵ֣י הַחֶ֔רֶב אֲשֶׁ֛ר אָנֹכִ֥י שֹׁלֵ֖חַ בֵּינֹתָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And they will drink and they will reel and they will act madly because of the sword that I [am] sending among them.

en.L: And they will drink, and they will reel and act like madmen because of the sword that I am sending among them."
en.B: When they drink, they will stagger and lose their minds because of the sword I am sending among them."
en.R: When they drink it, they will stagger around and act as if they were crazy. This will happen because of the war I am sending among them."

decisions.choice: reel and act madly: stagger and lose control, like drunken people
decisions.reason: The first verb means to sway back and forth; the second, to act like one out of his mind (51:7). The nations are thrown into helpless confusion.

decisions.choice: because of the sword: the picture of the cup is explained by real war
decisions.reason: The drunkenness stands for the effect of the war God sends: armies broken and peoples in panic. Verse 27 repeats the phrase.

decisions.choice: war
decisions.reason: Readable says "war" for "the sword", as the set wording for sword, famine and pestilence does in Jeremiah.

source.text: וָאֶקַּ֥ח אֶת־הַכּ֖וֹס מִיַּ֣ד יְהוָ֑ה וָֽאַשְׁקֶה֙ אֶת־כָּל־הַגּוֹיִ֔ם אֲשֶׁר־שְׁלָחַ֥נִי יְהוָ֖ה אֲלֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And I took the cup from [the] hand of Yahweh and I made drink all the nations that sent me Yahweh to them:

en.L: And I took the cup from the hand of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and made all the nations to whom {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent me drink [it]:
en.B: So I took the cup from the hand of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and made all the nations drink it to whom {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had sent me:
en.R: So I took the cup from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. I made all the nations {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sent me to drink from it. These are the ones who drank it:

decisions.choice: I took ... and made them drink: Jeremiah does as he is told
decisions.reason: The account uses the same verbs as the command in verse 15. The list of those who drank follows in verses 18-26, one long sentence.

decisions.choice: a colon at the end of the verse, with the list in verses 18-26
decisions.reason: The list of nations is the object of "made ... drink". Literal and Balanced end each verse of the list with a comma or semicolon; Readable supplies "These are the ones who drank it" and gives each group a short sentence.

source.text: אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ וְאֶת־עָרֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֔ה וְאֶת־מְלָכֶ֖יהָ אֶת־שָׂרֶ֑יהָ לָתֵ֨ת אֹתָ֜ם לְחָרְבָּ֧ה לְשַׁמָּ֛ה לִשְׁרֵקָ֥ה וְלִקְלָלָ֖ה כַּיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Jerusalem and [the] cities of Judah and its kings, its princes, to make them a ruin, a horror, a hissing and a curse, as the day this;

en.L: Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, and its kings [and] its princes, to make them a ruin, a horror, a hissing and a curse, as [it is] this day;
en.B: Jerusalem and the towns of Judah, its kings and its officials, to make them a ruin, a horror, an object of scorn and a curse, as they are today;
en.R: Jerusalem and the towns of Judah drank it, with their kings and leaders. It made them a ruin, a horror, something people mock and a curse, as they are today.

decisions.choice: Jerusalem first: judgment begins with God's own city
decisions.reason: The list starts with Jerusalem and Judah before it turns to the nations. Verse 29 gives the reason: if God begins with the city called by his name, the other nations cannot escape.

decisions.choice: a ruin, a horror, a hissing and a curse: a place destroyed, appalling, mocked and used as an example in curses
decisions.reason: As in verse 9 and 19:8. To become "a curse" is for one's name to be used when people curse, as in "may you be like them" (24:9; 29:22).

decisions.choice: as it is this day: the words look back on the judgment as already come
decisions.reason: The phrase means that the ruin had happened by the time these words were written down, which fits the book being gathered after Jerusalem fell. The Greek translation lacks it (see the note at 1:1; this is from general knowledge).

decisions.choice: princes (L), officials (B), leaders (R); a hissing (L), an object of scorn (B), something people mock (R)
decisions.reason: The set wording for *sar* and for this list. Readable supplies "drank it" and "It made them" to keep the list in short sentences.

source.text: אֶת־פַּרְעֹ֧ה מֶֽלֶךְ־מִצְרַ֛יִם וְאֶת־עֲבָדָ֥יו וְאֶת־שָׂרָ֖יו וְאֶת־כָּל־עַמּֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Pharaoh king of Egypt and his servants and his princes and all his people,

en.L: Pharaoh king of Egypt, and his servants, and his princes, and all his people,
en.B: Pharaoh king of Egypt, his servants, his officials and all his people,
en.R: Pharaoh king of Egypt drank it, with his officials, his leaders and all his people.

decisions.choice: Pharaoh king of Egypt: Pharaoh Neco, the king of that time
decisions.reason: In 605 BC the pharaoh was Neco II, who had killed Josiah (2 Kings 23:29) and whose army Nebuchadrezzar defeated that year at Carchemish (46:2). Egypt heads the foreign nations, from the south, and the list moves north and east to Babylon at the end.

decisions.choice: his servants and his princes: the members of his court and his high officials
decisions.reason: "Servants" here are a king's courtiers and officials, not household slaves.

decisions.choice: servants and princes (L); servants and officials (B); officials and leaders (R)
decisions.reason: The set wording for a king's servants and for *sar*. Balanced keeps "servants" so that the two words stay distinct.

source.text: וְאֵת֙ כָּל־הָעֶ֔רֶב וְאֵ֕ת כָּל־מַלְכֵ֖י אֶ֣רֶץ הָע֑וּץ וְאֵ֗ת כָּל־מַלְכֵי֙ אֶ֣רֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים וְאֶת־אַשְׁקְל֤וֹן וְאֶת־עַזָּה֙ וְאֶת־עֶקְר֔וֹן וְאֵ֖ת שְׁאֵרִ֥ית אַשְׁדּֽוֹד׃

records.literal_gloss: and all the mixed people, and all [the] kings of [the] land of the Uz, and all [the] kings of [the] land of [the] Philistines, and Ashkelon and Gaza and Ekron and [the] remnant of Ashdod;

en.L: and all the mixed people, and all the kings of the land of Uz, and all the kings of the land of the Philistines: Ashkelon and Gaza and Ekron and the remnant of Ashdod;
en.B: all the foreign peoples there; all the kings of the land of Uz; all the kings of the land of the Philistines, of Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron and what is left of Ashdod;
en.R: So did all the foreigners who lived in Egypt, and all the kings of the land of Uz. So did all the kings of the Philistines, in the cities of Ashkelon, Gaza and Ekron, and the people left in Ashdod.

decisions.choice: the mixed people: foreigners living among the Egyptians
decisions.reason: The word means a mixture of peoples. With Egypt it most likely means the foreign groups settled there, such as hired soldiers and traders (compare 50:37; Exodus 12:38, where the same word is used of the mixed crowd leaving Egypt).

decisions.choice: the land of Uz: a region east or south-east of Judah, near Edom
decisions.reason: Uz is the homeland of Job (Job 1:1). Lamentations 4:21 links it with Edom, and Genesis 36:28 lists Uz among the descendants of Seir in Edom.

decisions.choice: Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron and the remnant of Ashdod: the Philistine cities that still stood
decisions.reason: Gath, the fifth Philistine city, is missing; it had lost its importance long before (Amos 6:2). Ashdod is called a "remnant" because it had been badly weakened by war, in particular a long Egyptian siege in the seventh century BC (this is from general knowledge).

decisions.choice: all the foreign peoples there (B); all the foreigners who lived in Egypt (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show that this group belongs with Egypt (m1). Readable supplies "So did" and "the cities of".

source.text: אֶת־אֱד֥וֹם וְאֶת־מוֹאָ֖ב וְאֶת־בְּנֵ֥י עַמּֽוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: Edom and Moab and [the] sons of Ammon,

en.L: Edom and Moab and the {{gender:children|sons}} of Ammon,
en.B: Edom, Moab and the Ammonites,
en.R: Then Edom, Moab and the Ammonites drank it.

decisions.choice: Edom, Moab and Ammon: Judah's neighbors to the south-east and east, across the Jordan and the Dead Sea
decisions.reason: The three are often named together as Judah's kin and rivals (9:25; 27:3). Jeremiah gives each its own oracle in chapters 48-49.

decisions.choice: the Ammonites
decisions.reason: As in 9:25, "sons of Ammon" is the people of Ammon. Literal keeps the Hebrew form with the gender setting.

source.text: וְאֵת֙ כָּל־מַלְכֵי־צֹ֔ר וְאֵ֖ת כָּל־מַלְכֵ֣י צִיד֑וֹן וְאֵת֙ מַלְכֵ֣י הָאִ֔י אֲשֶׁ֖ר בְּעֵ֥בֶר הַיָּֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: and all [the] kings of Tyre and all [the] kings of Sidon and [the] kings of the coastland that [is] across the sea;

en.L: and all the kings of Tyre, and all the kings of Sidon, and the kings of the coastland that [is] across the sea;
en.B: all the kings of Tyre and all the kings of Sidon; the kings of the coastlands across the sea;
en.R: So did all the kings of Tyre and Sidon, and the kings of the lands across the sea.

decisions.choice: Tyre and Sidon, and the coastland across the sea: the Phoenician cities and their settlements over the Mediterranean
decisions.reason: Tyre and Sidon were the great trading ports on the coast north of Israel (47:4). The coastland across the sea most likely means their colonies and trading posts overseas, such as Cyprus.

decisions.choice: the lands across the sea
decisions.reason: As in Isaiah, Readable says "lands" for the coastland far away.

source.text: וְאֶת־דְּדָ֤ן וְאֶת־תֵּימָא֙ וְאֶת־בּ֔וּז וְאֵ֖ת כָּל־קְצוּצֵ֥י פֵאָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: and Dedan and Tema and Buz and all [who are] clipped [at the] corner;

en.L: and Dedan and Tema and Buz, and all who are clipped [at the] corners;
en.B: Dedan, Tema and Buz, and all who clip the hair at their temples;
en.R: So did the tribes of Dedan, Tema and Buz, and all the tribes who cut their hair short at the sides.

decisions.choice: Dedan, Tema and Buz: Arab tribes and oasis towns of the north Arabian desert
decisions.reason: Dedan and Tema appear among the descendants of Abraham (Genesis 25:3, 15) and as desert caravan peoples (Isaiah 21:13-14). Buz was a son of Abraham's brother Nahor (Genesis 22:21), and Elihu in Job was a Buzite (Job 32:2).

decisions.choice: all who are clipped at the corners: desert tribes who cut the hair at their temples
decisions.reason: As in 9:25 (and 49:32). These peoples trimmed the hair at the sides of the head, a custom Israel was forbidden (Leviticus 19:27).

decisions.choice: the wording of 9:25
decisions.reason: The same phrase keeps the same wording as in 9:25. Readable supplies "the tribes of".

source.text: וְאֵ֖ת כָּל־מַלְכֵ֣י עֲרָ֑ב וְאֵת֙ כָּל־מַלְכֵ֣י הָעֶ֔רֶב הַשֹּׁכְנִ֖ים בַּמִּדְבָּֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: and all [the] kings of Arabia and all [the] kings of the mixed people who dwell in the wilderness;

en.L: and all the kings of Arabia, and all the kings of the mixed peoples who dwell in the wilderness;
en.B: all the kings of Arabia and all the kings of the mixed peoples who live in the desert;
en.R: So did all the kings of Arabia and all the kings of the other peoples who live in the desert.

decisions.choice: the Hebrew as it stands, with both "Arabia" and "the mixed peoples"
alternatives: one phrase only: all the kings of Arabia who live in the desert
decisions.reason: In Hebrew the words for Arabia and for "mixed people" are written with the same three consonants. The second phrase may be an accidental repeat of the first, made when a scribe copied the same word twice with different vowels, and the Greek translation seems to have only one of them (this is from general knowledge). As it stands the verse names the kings of Arabia and the kings of other desert peoples.

decisions.choice: Arabia: the tribes of the Arabian desert
decisions.reason: The name means the desert peoples to the east and south, not a single kingdom.

source.text: וְאֵ֣ת׀כָּל־מַלְכֵ֣י זִמְרִ֗י וְאֵת֙ כָּל־מַלְכֵ֣י עֵילָ֔ם וְאֵ֖ת כָּל־מַלְכֵ֥י מָדָֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: and all [the] kings of Zimri and all [the] kings of Elam and all [the] kings of Media;

en.L: and all the kings of Zimri, and all the kings of Elam, and all the kings of Media;
en.B: all the kings of Zimri, all the kings of Elam and all the kings of Media;
en.R: So did all the kings of Zimri, Elam and Media.

decisions.choice: Zimri: an unknown people
decisions.reason: No people called Zimri is known elsewhere. It may be connected with Zimran, a son of Abraham and Keturah (Genesis 25:2), whose descendants would be an eastern desert people. It has also been explained as a disguised name, made by the same letter-swapping as Sheshach in verse 26. The Greek translation lacks the name (this is from general knowledge).

decisions.choice: Elam and Media: kingdoms east of Babylon, in what is now Iran
decisions.reason: Elam lay east of Babylonia (49:34-39). Media lay to the north-east; the Medes later joined in the attack on Babylon (51:11, 28). The list now reaches the far east of the known world.

source.text: וְאֵ֣ת׀כָּל־מַלְכֵ֣י הַצָּפ֗וֹן הַקְּרֹבִ֤ים וְהָֽרְחֹקִים֙ אִ֣ישׁ אֶל־אָחִ֔יו וְאֵת֙ כָּל־הַמַּמְלְכ֣וֹת הָאָ֔רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֖ר עַל־פְּנֵ֣י הָאֲדָמָ֑ה וּמֶ֥לֶךְ שֵׁשַׁ֖ךְ יִשְׁתֶּ֥ה אַחֲרֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: and all [the] kings of the north, the near and the far, each to his brother, and all the kingdoms of the earth which [are] on [the] face of the ground; and [the] king of Sheshach will drink after them.

en.L: and all the kings of the north, the near and the far, one after another, and all the kingdoms of the world that [are] on the face of the earth. And the king of Sheshach will drink after them.
en.B: and all the kings of the north, near and far, one after another, and all the kingdoms of the world on the face of the earth. And after them the king of Sheshach will drink.
en.R: So did all the kings of the north, near and far, one after another. Every kingdom on the face of the earth drank it. And last of all, the king of Sheshach, that is, Babylon, will drink it.

decisions.choice: Sheshach: a coded name for Babylon
decisions.reason: Sheshach is Babylon written in a simple code called *atbash*, in which the first letter of the alphabet stands for the last, the second for the next to last, and so on. By that code the consonants of Babel become those of Sheshach. In 51:41 Sheshach stands in parallel with Babylon, which confirms the meaning, and 51:1 uses the same code for the Chaldeans. Since Babylon is named openly elsewhere, the code was probably not for secrecy; it may be a play on words or a mark of contempt. The Greek translation lacks this sentence (this is from general knowledge).

decisions.choice: will drink after them: the king of Babylon, God's instrument, will drink the cup last
decisions.reason: The nations Babylon conquers drink first; then Babylon itself must drink, as verses 12-14 have said. The verb changes from past to future: the list of those who drank ends with what will still happen.

decisions.choice: each to his brother: one after another
decisions.reason: The idiom means each in turn, one following the next.

decisions.choice: the king of Sheshach, that is, Babylon
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the name and adds what it stands for, since most readers would not recognize the code (m1). Literal and Balanced keep the name alone, with the footnote.

source.text: וְאָמַרְתָּ֣ אֲלֵיהֶ֡םסכֹּֽה־אָמַר֩ יְהוָ֨ה צְבָא֜וֹת אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל שְׁת֤וּ וְשִׁכְרוּ֙ וּקְי֔וּ וְנִפְל֖וּ וְלֹ֣א תָק֑וּמוּ מִפְּנֵ֣י הַחֶ֔רֶב אֲשֶׁ֛ר אָנֹכִ֥י שֹׁלֵ֖חַ בֵּינֵיכֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And you will say to them: Thus says Yahweh of hosts [the] God of Israel: Drink and be drunk and vomit and fall and not you will rise because of the sword that I [am] sending among you.

en.L: "And you shall say to them, 'Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts, the God of Israel: Drink and be drunk and vomit, and fall, and you will not rise, because of the sword that I am sending among you.'
en.B: "Then say to them, '{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, the God of Israel, says this: Drink and get drunk and vomit; fall down and do not get up again, because of the sword I am sending among you.'
en.R: "Then tell them, 'This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, the God of Israel, says: Drink until you are drunk and throw up. Fall down and never get up again, because of the war I am sending among you.'

decisions.choice: and you shall say to them: the LORD's instructions to Jeremiah, broken off in verse 16, go on
decisions.reason: After the list of nations (verses 17-26), the LORD's words to Jeremiah resume. They continue to the end of the chapter: what Jeremiah is to say to the nations (verses 27-29), and the poem he is to speak against them (verses 30-38).

decisions.choice: drink, be drunk, vomit, fall and not rise: the picture of the cup carried to its end
decisions.reason: Each step takes the drinker further into helplessness, until he falls and cannot get up. The meaning is defeat in war from which there is no recovery, as "because of the sword" makes clear (verse 16).

decisions.choice: double quotation marks for the LORD's words to Jeremiah, single for the message to the nations
decisions.reason: The LORD's speech reopens here and runs to the end of the chapter. The words Jeremiah is to say take single quotation marks, as in 13:12-14, and "Thus says the LORD" inside them is followed by a colon. Readable says "war" for "the sword", as in verse 16.

decisions.choice: the LORD of Armies
decisions.reason: As in verse 8.

source.text: וְהָיָ֗ה כִּ֧י יְמָאֲנ֛וּ לָקַֽחַת־הַכּ֥וֹס מִיָּדְךָ֖ לִשְׁתּ֑וֹת וְאָמַרְתָּ֣ אֲלֵיהֶ֗ם כֹּ֥ה אָמַ֛ר יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת שָׁת֥וֹ תִשְׁתּֽוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And it will be, if they refuse to take the cup from your hand to drink, and you will say to them: Thus says Yahweh of hosts: Surely you will drink.

en.L: And if they refuse to take the cup from your hand to drink, then you shall say to them, 'Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts: You shall surely drink!
en.B: If they will not take the cup from your hand and drink, say to them, '{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies says this: You must drink it!
en.R: They may refuse to take the cup from you and drink it. If they do, tell them, 'This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies says: You have no choice. You must drink it!

decisions.choice: surely you will drink: the doubled verb makes it certain; there is no refusing
decisions.reason: The Hebrew repeats the verb for emphasis. Refusing the cup does not avoid it: the judgment is decided.

decisions.choice: You have no choice
decisions.reason: Readable gives the force of the doubled verb in plain words.

source.text: כִּי֩ הִנֵּ֨ה בָעִ֜יר אֲשֶׁ֧ר נִֽקְרָא־שְׁמִ֣י עָלֶ֗יהָ אָֽנֹכִי֙ מֵחֵ֣ל לְהָרַ֔ע וְאַתֶּ֖ם הִנָּקֵ֣ה תִנָּק֑וּ לֹ֣א תִנָּק֔וּ כִּ֣י חֶ֗רֶב אֲנִ֤י קֹרֵא֙ עַל־כָּל־יֹשְׁבֵ֣י הָאָ֔רֶץ נְאֻ֖ם יְהוָ֥ה צְבָאֽוֹת׃

records.literal_gloss: For look, on the city which is called my name on it I [am] beginning to do harm, and you, being held innocent will you be held innocent? Not you will be held innocent, for a sword I [am] calling on all [the] inhabitants of the earth, declaration of Yahweh of hosts.

en.L: For look, I am beginning to bring disaster on the city that is called by {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name, and you, will you indeed go unpunished? You will not go unpunished, for I am summoning a sword against all the inhabitants of the earth, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts.'
en.B: For see, I am starting to bring disaster on the city that bears {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name. Do you really think you will go unpunished? You will not go unpunished, for I am calling for a sword against everyone who lives on the earth, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies.'
en.R: Look, I am beginning to bring disaster on Jerusalem, the city that belongs to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. So do you think you will escape punishment? You will not escape! I am calling for war against everyone on earth, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies.'

decisions.choice: the city called by my name: Jerusalem, the city that belongs to God
decisions.reason: To have someone's name called over a thing is to belong to them. The temple is "the house called by my name" (7:10-11), and Jerusalem is the city that bears God's name.

decisions.choice: if God begins with his own city, the nations will not escape
decisions.reason: The argument moves from the greater to the lesser: if judgment begins with the people who bear God's name, those who never knew him cannot expect to be spared. The same reasoning appears in 49:12 and 1 Peter 4:17.

decisions.choice: be held innocent: go free of punishment
decisions.reason: The verb means to be declared free of guilt and so left unpunished (Exodus 34:7; Jeremiah 49:12). The doubled form makes the question sharp: will you really get off?

decisions.choice: Jerusalem, the city that belongs to me
decisions.reason: Readable names the city and explains the idiom (m1). The message to the nations closes here; the LORD's words to Jeremiah continue in verse 30.

source.text: וְאַתָּה֙ תִּנָּבֵ֣א אֲלֵיהֶ֔ם אֵ֥ת כָּל־הַדְּבָרִ֖ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה וְאָמַרְתָּ֣ אֲלֵיהֶ֗ם יְהוָ֞ה מִמָּר֤וֹם יִשְׁאָג֙ וּמִמְּע֤וֹן קָדְשׁוֹ֙ יִתֵּ֣ן קוֹל֔וֹ שָׁאֹ֤ג יִשְׁאַג֙ עַל־נָוֵ֔הוּ הֵידָד֙ כְּדֹרְכִ֣ים יַֽעֲנֶ֔ה אֶ֥ל כָּל־יֹשְׁבֵ֖י הָאָֽרֶץ׃

records.literal_gloss: And you, you will prophesy to them all the words these, and you will say to them: Yahweh from on high will roar, and from [the] dwelling of his holiness he will give his voice; roaring he will roar against his pasture; a shout like treaders he will answer to all [the] inhabitants of the earth.

en.L: And you, prophesy against them all these words, and say to them: \q '{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} roars from on high, \q and from {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} holy dwelling {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} utters {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} voice; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} roars mightily against {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} fold; \q a shout like those who tread [grapes] \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} raises against all the inhabitants of the earth.
en.B: As for you, prophesy all these words against them. Tell them: \q '{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} roars from on high; \q from {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} holy dwelling {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} raises {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} voice. \q He roars and roars against {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own pasture; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} shouts like those who tread the grapes, \q a shout against all who live on the earth.
en.R: So prophesy all these words against them. Tell them: \q '{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will roar like a lion from heaven. \q He will thunder from {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} holy home. \q He will roar loudly against the land where {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} flock grazes. \q He will shout like people stamping on grapes to make wine. \q He will shout against everyone who lives on the earth.

decisions.choice: the LORD roars from on high: the LORD as a lion roaring before it attacks
decisions.reason: The words echo Amos 1:2 and Joel 4:16, where the LORD roars from Zion. Here he roars "from on high", from his dwelling in heaven, against the whole earth. The lion picture returns in verse 38.

decisions.choice: his pasture: the land where God's own flock lives
decisions.reason: The word means a pasture or fold for sheep. It most likely means God's own land and people, as in 10:25, where "his pasture" is Jacob's home. The flock and its shepherds return in verses 34-38. It could also mean God's own dwelling place, but the shepherd picture of the poem favors the pasture.

decisions.choice: a shout like those who tread grapes: the shout of the grape harvest turned into a battle cry
decisions.reason: Grapes were trodden underfoot in a winepress, with rhythmic shouts (48:33; Isaiah 16:9-10). The same shout here is the war cry of judgment, and treading the grapes is a picture of crushing the nations (Isaiah 63:2-3; Joel 4:13).

decisions.choice: the poem of verses 30-38 is the message Jeremiah is to speak
decisions.reason: The verse begins with the LORD's instruction to Jeremiah and then gives the words he is to say, a poem that runs to the end of the chapter.

decisions.choice: like a lion; from heaven
decisions.reason: Readable says "like a lion" to make clear what roaring means here (m1), and "from heaven" for "from on high". It explains "his pasture" as the land where God's flock grazes (m2). Literal supplies "[grapes]".

decisions.choice: the poem set in lines, opening single quotation marks
decisions.reason: The words Jeremiah is to say are a poem and are set in lines; they take single quotation marks inside the LORD's speech, closing at the end of verse 38.

source.text: בָּ֤א שָׁאוֹן֙ עַד־קְצֵ֣ה הָאָ֔רֶץ כִּ֣י רִ֤יב לַֽיהוָה֙ בַּגּוֹיִ֔ם נִשְׁפָּ֥ט ה֖וּא לְכָל־בָּשָׂ֑ר הָרְשָׁעִ֛ים נְתָנָ֥ם לַחֶ֖רֶב נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Has come an uproar to [the] end of the earth, for a lawsuit [belongs] to Yahweh with [the] nations; he is entering into judgment with all flesh; the wicked he has given them to the sword, declaration of Yahweh.

en.L: An uproar has come to the end of the earth, \q for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has a lawsuit with the nations; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is entering into judgment with all flesh; \q the wicked {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has given to the sword, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: The uproar reaches to the end of the earth, \q for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has a case against the nations. \q He is bringing all humankind to judgment, \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} hands the wicked over to the sword, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: The noise of battle will reach the ends of the earth. \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is taking the nations to court. \q He will judge all people. \q He will hand the wicked over to be killed in war, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: a lawsuit with the nations: God brings a legal case against them as judge
decisions.reason: The word is used for a dispute brought to court (2:9; Hosea 4:1; Micah 6:2). God both accuses the nations and judges them; the next line says he is "entering into judgment".

decisions.choice: all flesh: all humankind
decisions.reason: "Flesh" means human beings in their weakness and mortality (12:12; Isaiah 40:5-6).

decisions.choice: has come ... has given: what God has decided is spoken of as already done
decisions.reason: The verbs are in the form for completed action, though the judgment is still to come. Prophets often speak this way of what God has settled.

decisions.choice: a lawsuit (L); a case (B); taking ... to court (R); all humankind (B), all people (R)
decisions.reason: Each level keeps the court picture. Balanced and Readable say "humankind" and "people" for "flesh"; Readable says "the noise of battle" for the uproar and "killed in war" for "given to the sword".

source.text: כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת הִנֵּ֥ה רָעָ֛ה יֹצֵ֖את מִגּ֣וֹי אֶל־גּ֑וֹי וְסַ֣עַר גָּד֔וֹל יֵע֖וֹר מִיַּרְכְּתֵי־אָֽרֶץ׃

records.literal_gloss: Thus says Yahweh of hosts: Look, disaster [is] going out from nation to nation, and a storm great is stirred up from [the] farthest parts of [the] earth.

en.L: Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts: \q Look, disaster is going out from nation to nation, \q and a great storm is stirred up \q from the farthest parts of the earth.
en.B: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies says this: \q Look! Disaster is spreading from nation to nation, \q and a great storm is rising \q from the far ends of the earth.
en.R: This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies says: \q Disaster is spreading from one nation to another. \q A great storm is rising \q from the far corners of the earth.

decisions.choice: disaster going out from nation to nation: judgment spreading like the cup passed from one to the next
decisions.reason: The word means calamity, not moral evil. It passes from nation to nation as the cup did in verses 17-26.

decisions.choice: a great storm from the farthest parts of the earth: the invader pictured as a storm
decisions.reason: The same words describe the army from the north in 6:22, and the storm of the LORD's anger in 23:19 and 30:23.

decisions.choice: the LORD of Armies
decisions.reason: As in verse 8.

source.text: וְהָי֞וּ חַֽלְלֵ֤י יְהוָה֙ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֔וּא מִקְצֵ֥ה הָאָ֖רֶץ וְעַד־קְצֵ֣ה הָאָ֑רֶץ לֹ֣א יִסָּפְד֗וּ וְלֹ֤א יֵאָֽסְפוּ֙ וְלֹ֣א יִקָּבֵ֔רוּ לְדֹ֛מֶן עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הָאֲדָמָ֖ה יִֽהְיֽוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And will be [the] slain of Yahweh on the day that from [the] end of the earth and to [the] end of the earth; not they will be mourned and not they will be gathered and not they will be buried; dung on [the] face of the ground they will be.

en.L: And the slain of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will be on that day \q from the end of the earth to the end of the earth; \q they will not be mourned, nor gathered, nor buried; \q they will be dung on the face of the ground.
en.B: On that day those slain by {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will lie \q from one end of the earth to the other. \q No one will mourn them or gather them or bury them; \q they will be like dung lying on the ground.
en.R: At that time the people whom {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has struck down will lie everywhere, \q from one end of the earth to the other. \q No one will mourn for them, gather up their bodies or bury them. \q They will lie on the ground like dung.

decisions.choice: the slain of the LORD: those killed in the LORD's judgment
decisions.reason: The phrase means those who die in the war God sends (Isaiah 66:16), not people killed by God's own hand apart from it.

decisions.choice: not mourned, gathered or buried: the worst disgrace for the dead
decisions.reason: To lie unburied, with no one to mourn, was the deepest shame in the ancient world. Jeremiah uses the same words of Judah's dead (8:2; 16:4), and now of the nations.

decisions.choice: like dung (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "like" to make the picture a comparison; Literal keeps the bare Hebrew. Readable says "struck down" and "their bodies".

source.text: הֵילִ֨ילוּ הָרֹעִ֜ים וְזַעֲק֗וּ וְהִֽתְפַּלְּשׁוּ֙ אַדִּירֵ֣י הַצֹּ֔אן כִּֽי־מָלְא֥וּ יְמֵיכֶ֖ם לִטְב֑וֹחַ וּתְפוֹצ֣וֹתִיכֶ֔ם וּנְפַלְתֶּ֖ם כִּכְלִ֥י חֶמְדָּֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Wail, the shepherds, and cry out, and roll, nobles of the flock, for are fulfilled your days for slaughtering, and your scatterings, and you will fall like a vessel of desire.

en.L: Wail, you shepherds, and cry out, \q and roll [in the dust], you nobles of the flock, \q for your days for slaughter have been fulfilled, \q and your scatterings, and you will fall like a precious vessel.
en.B: Wail, you shepherds! Cry out! \q Roll in the dust, you leaders of the flock! \q The time has come for you to be slaughtered and scattered, \q and you will fall and break like a precious jar.
en.R: Cry out in grief, you shepherds who rule the people! Shout! \q Roll in the dust, you leaders of the flock! \q The time has come for you to be killed and scattered. \q You will fall and break like a valuable pot.

decisions.choice: shepherds, nobles of the flock: the rulers of the nations
decisions.reason: Kings and leaders are called shepherds throughout Jeremiah (2:8; 10:21; 23:1-4). The "nobles of the flock" are the strongest of the herd, the leading men. Their flock is their people.

decisions.choice: roll in the dust: a sign of deep mourning
decisions.reason: Mourners rolled in dust or ashes (6:26; Micah 1:10). The verb has no object here; the dust is understood.

decisions.choice: your scatterings: an uncertain word, most likely meaning that they will be scattered
decisions.reason: The Hebrew form here is unusual. It may be a noun, "your scatterings", joined loosely to "your days for slaughter", or a verb, "I will scatter you". Either way it adds being scattered to being slaughtered.

decisions.choice: like a precious vessel: a fine jar that shatters when it falls
decisions.reason: The Hebrew compares the leaders to a costly vessel dropped and broken (22:28). The Greek translation reads "like choice rams", from Hebrew letters very close to those of "like a vessel", which would keep the picture of a slaughtered flock (this is from general knowledge).

decisions.choice: Wail (L, B), Cry out in grief (R); nobles (L), leaders (B, R); fall and break (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Wail" follows the set wording from Isaiah. Balanced and Readable add "break" to show what happens to a vessel that falls, and Readable adds "who rule the people" to explain the shepherd picture (m1). Literal supplies "[in the dust]" (m2).

source.text: וְאָבַ֥ד מָנ֖וֹס מִן־הָֽרֹעִ֑ים וּפְלֵיטָ֖ה מֵאַדִּירֵ֥י הַצֹּֽאן׃

records.literal_gloss: And will perish flight from the shepherds, and escape from [the] nobles of the flock.

en.L: And flight will perish from the shepherds, \q and escape from the nobles of the flock.
en.B: The shepherds will have nowhere to flee, \q the leaders of the flock no way to escape.
en.R: The shepherds will have no place to run to. \q The leaders of the flock will not escape.

decisions.choice: flight will perish from the shepherds: there will be no way of escape
decisions.reason: "Flight" here means a place or way to flee. To say it "perishes" is to say it is gone (Amos 2:14). The leaders who should protect the flock cannot even save themselves.

decisions.choice: nowhere to flee (B); no place to run to (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the idiom; Literal keeps its form.

source.text: ק֚וֹל צַעֲקַ֣ת הָֽרֹעִ֔ים וִֽילְלַ֖ת אַדִּירֵ֣י הַצֹּ֑אן כִּֽי־שֹׁדֵ֥ד יְהוָ֖ה אֶת־מַרְעִיתָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: [The] sound of [the] cry of the shepherds and [the] wailing of [the] nobles of the flock, for [is] destroying Yahweh their pasture.

en.L: The sound of the cry of the shepherds, \q and the wailing of the nobles of the flock! \q For {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is destroying their pasture.
en.B: Listen to the shepherds crying out, \q the leaders of the flock wailing, \q for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is laying waste their pasture.
en.R: Listen! The shepherds are crying out. \q The leaders of the flock are wailing, \q because {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is destroying their pasture.

decisions.choice: the sound of: an exclamation, "Listen!"
decisions.reason: The word for "sound" or "voice" can stand alone at the start of a sentence to call attention to what is heard (3:21; 4:15; Isaiah 40:3).

decisions.choice: their pasture: the land and people the rulers were responsible for
decisions.reason: The pasture is the land where their flock lives (verse 30). When the LORD destroys it, the shepherds have nothing left to rule.

decisions.choice: Listen
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the exclamation as "Listen"; Literal keeps the bare noun.

source.text: וְנָדַ֖מּוּ נְא֣וֹת הַשָּׁל֑וֹם מִפְּנֵ֖י חֲר֥וֹן אַף־יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And are devastated [the] pastures of the peace because of [the] burning of [the] anger of Yahweh.

en.L: And the peaceful pastures are laid waste \q because of the burning anger of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: The peaceful meadows lie in ruins \q because of the fierce anger of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: The quiet fields where the flocks grazed in safety are ruined, \q because {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is burning with anger.

decisions.choice: laid waste: ruined and left silent
decisions.reason: The verb can mean either to be destroyed or to be made silent; here both fit, as the once peaceful pastures fall still and empty (compare 8:14; 48:2).

decisions.choice: the pastures of peace: pastures where flocks grazed safely
decisions.reason: "Peace" here means safety and well-being, the quiet of land at rest.

decisions.choice: burning anger (L); fierce anger (B); burning with anger (R)
decisions.reason: As in 4:8. Readable explains "pastures of peace" as fields where the flocks grazed in safety (m2).

source.text: עָזַ֥ב כַּכְּפִ֖יר סֻכּ֑וֹ כִּֽי־הָיְתָ֤ה אַרְצָם֙ לְשַׁמָּ֔ה מִפְּנֵי֙ חֲר֣וֹן הַיּוֹנָ֔ה וּמִפְּנֵ֖י חֲר֥וֹן אַפּֽוֹ׃פ

records.literal_gloss: He has left like the young lion his lair, for has become their land a horror because of [the] burning of the oppressor and because of [the] burning of his anger.

en.L: Like a young lion {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has left {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} lair, \q for their land has become a horror \q because of the burning of the oppressor, \q and because of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} burning anger.'"
en.B: Like a lion {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has left {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} den, \q and their land has become a desolate waste \q because of the fury of the oppressor \q and because of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} fierce anger.'"
en.R: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has come out like a lion leaving its den to hunt. \q Their land has become an empty waste \q because of the cruel enemy's fury \q and because of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} burning anger.'"

decisions.choice: like a young lion he has left his lair: the LORD has gone out to attack
decisions.reason: The subject is not named. In the poem it is most likely the LORD, who roared like a lion in verse 30; Jeremiah pictures God as a lion coming up against the nations in 49:19 and 50:44 (compare Hosea 5:14). In 4:7 the lion is the invader, and some take it so here, or take the lion as the LORD leaving his own land to its fate. The verse then ends with "his burning anger", which in the light of verse 37 is the LORD's.

decisions.choice: the burning of the oppressor: the fury of the cruel enemy
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has "the burning of the oppressor", using the word for burning anger without the word for anger. Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Greek translation read "the sword of the oppressor", as in 46:16 and 50:16, which may be the original wording. The word for "oppressor" is spelled like the word for "dove", and some ancient translations read it that way. These statements come from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: a horror: a desolate place that appalls those who see it
decisions.reason: As in verse 11.

decisions.choice: The LORD ... to hunt; the cruel enemy
decisions.reason: Readable names the LORD as the lion (m1) and says what the lion goes out to do. It says "the cruel enemy" for "the oppressor". Balanced says "a desolate waste" and Readable "an empty waste" for the land, as in verse 11. The poem and the LORD's speech both close here.
